description: Test your knowledge of Chemistry & Metabolism of Proteins and Immunology.

cards.text: What are the four groups bonded to the alpha-carbon of every amino acid?
cards.answer: Amino group (-NH2), carboxyl group (-COOH), hydrogen atom (-H), and a variable side chain (R group). The R group is what makes each amino acid unique.

tip.tip: Remember: ACHS — Alpha-Carbon Has 4 things Stuck

cards.text: Why do amino acids exist as zwitterions at physiological pH 7.4?
cards.answer: At pH 7.4, the amino group is protonated (-NH3+) and the carboxyl group is deprotonated (-COO-), making amino acids carry both positive and negative charges simultaneously.

tip.tip: Zwitter = both charges = +NH3+ and -COO- at the same time

cards.text: List the 9 essential amino acids using the mnemonic PVT TIM HALL.
cards.answer: Phenylalanine, Valine, Tryptophan, Threonine, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Arginine (semi-essential), Leucine, Lysine. These cannot be synthesised by the body and must come from diet.

tip.tip: PVT TIM HALL = Private Tim Hall (military rank) — they must be supplied from outside (diet)

cards.text: What is the metabolic defect in phenylketonuria (PKU) and why does dietary restriction work?
cards.answer: PKU is the inability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine accumulates and damages the brain. A Phe-restricted diet prevents accumulation while dietary tyrosine becomes the essential source.

tip.tip: Phe → Tyr broken = supply Phe from diet (restricted) + Tyr as supplement (essential now)

cards.text: What type of bond links amino acids together in a protein chain, and what is released?
cards.answer: A peptide bond — a covalent bond formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. Water (H2O) is released during this condensation reaction.

tip.tip: Peptide = Peptide bond; water leaves = condensation (condensation = water leaves)

cards.text: How does a single amino acid change cause sickle cell disease, and why does this illustrate the importance of primary structure?
cards.answer: In sickle cell disease, glutamic acid (Glu, negatively charged) at position 6 of beta-globin is replaced by valine (Val, hydrophobic). One amino acid change out of 146 alters the entire protein's behaviour, causing polymerisation and sickling.

tip.tip: 1 amino acid changed = 1 disease. Primary structure = the blueprint — one typo breaks everything

cards.text: Distinguish between alpha-helix and beta-sheet secondary structures with an example of each.
cards.answer: Alpha-helix: polypeptide coils into a right-handed spiral (3.6 amino acids per turn), found in keratin (hair, nails). Beta-sheet: chain zigzags back and forth in flat sheets, found in silk fibroin. Both stabilised by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms.

tip.tip: Helix = spiral staircase (keratin = hair spiral); Sheet = folded paper (silk = smooth sheets)

cards.text: What four types of interactions determine tertiary structure, and which is the strongest?
cards.answer: Hydrophobic interactions (non-polar R-groups cluster inside), hydrogen bonds (polar R-groups), ionic bonds (charged R-groups), and disulfide bonds (S-S between cysteines). Disulfide bonds are the strongest — they are covalent links.

tip.tip: Tertiary = 3D fold of ONE chain; Disulfide = the heavyweight (only covalent bond in tertiary structure)
